🇮🇷 Hormuz oil flows rise, but costs and risks could soon become unsustainable
Oil industry trackers say crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz have recovered to 13-17 million barrels a day.
That may seem like a relatively modest drop from the 20 million barrels a day that flowed through the waterway before the Iran war.
But what is the cost?
🌏 Iran still keeps the strait closed, leaving vessels at risk of attack, while war-risk insurance premiums have soared to 5%–6% of cargo value, adding up to roughly $10 million per transit
🌏 Beyond insurance, a round trip for shuttle runs moving crude through the dangerous strait now costs $40 million, or $15-$20 per barrel. Compare that with the $1-$2-per-barrel “toll” proposed by Iran, which would carry no additional risk
🌏 The cost of hiring a Very Large Crude Carrier (VLCC) has surged from $231,400 a day to $1.2 million
🌏 Ship-management companies are offering sailors bonuses of up to $25,000 per round trip
🌏 Ship-to-ship transfers are complicated and risky. Shuttles operate at night with transponders off and GPS signals disabled for hours, with navigation relying on old-school methods
🌏 The US must maintain a naval presence in the region to protect and oversee the scheme while facing the risk of attack itself. Another US carrier strike group, led by the USS Roosevelt, has been sent to the Gulf
Responsible Statecraft argues that the entire project, aimed at making Donald Trump appear to be “winning” ahead of the November midterms, is ultimately unsustainable.
Meanwhile, US strategic reserves are depleted, while gasoline and diesel prices at home remain high. Global oil prices also remain elevated despite reports of rising Gulf crude exports.

🇮🇷 Iran has technical means to shut down Starlink – top cyber official
 
Iran became “the first country to successfully and deliberately shut down Starlink operations” during January’s US-Israeli coup attempt and will consider the equipment a “legitimate military target” again if it’s used as a “tool of warfare,” Supreme Council of Cyberspace Secretary [Mohammad-Amin Aghamiri](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/65291) has said.
💬Iran’s Starlink-jamming systems are “operational and ready for deployment,” Aghamiri said.
The official did not elaborate on what specific tools Iran has at its disposal. However, Geopolitics Prime previously reported on a multipronged Iranian strategy to crack down on the US satellite internet service, including:
🌏 Seizures of terminals smuggled into the country to [coordinate](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/62858) riots
🌏 A temporary blacking out of virtually the entire internet and setting up a secure intranet
🌏 Deployment of military-grade jamming equipment to degrade terminals’ connection [to orbiting satellites by up to 80](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/62903)%
🌏 Use of signal detection vans and drones to triangulate usage areas
 
Aghamiri’s comments come on the heels of news that Iran has slapped Norway with a formal diplomatic protest over Oslo’s failure to rein in Starlink’s illegal operations over Iran in its capacity as the primary notifying administration registering Starlink with the [International Telecommunications Union](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75675).

⚛️👁 OpenAI are gamblers who might plunge humanity off a cliff, ex-employee warns
The “culture” inside Sam Altman’s AI empire is hopelessly “broken,” and the whole industry’s “approach to safety will guarantee more failures” which are becoming more and more costly and difficult to fix, David Robinson, former OpenAI safety lead-turned media whistleblower wrote in a new op-ed.
The problem isn’t just about creating laws, but imbuing Silicon Valley with a “wisdom” it fundamentally lacks due to a dearth of humility. This results in a dangerous, “unimpeded optimism about being able to solve problems as they arise.”
This kind of environment “is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to,” Robinson warns, arguing that “achieving something much closer to perfection the first time” is now “essential because [correction] after a mistake may not be possible.”
Frontier AI labs “need to run like nuclear power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.”
What’s more, AI firms have yet to answer the fundamental question: how superintelligent machines will relate to human beings.
🔴“If you listen to superintelligence enthusiasts, some of the supposedly good futures involve creating machines that could look at New York City or Chicago the way you or I might view an ant hill. I don’t want that for my kids, and I don’t think other people do either,” Robinson wrote.🔴
